concepts.name: Choosing the swap target
concepts.summary: The concept swapped in is drawn from the same category as the one swapped out, and in the report experiments it is restricted to items the model was not already likely to say.
concepts.explanation: A swap is informative only if the answer it produces could not have arrived without it. In the think-of-a-category experiment the target item is drawn from the same category as the model's spontaneous choice and restricted to items outside the top ten of the model's possible outputs, so a flip cannot be put down to the target already sitting near the top. In the two-hop experiments the swap target is chosen at random from within the same category as the true intermediate. In the flexible-generalization protocol four arguments per category give twelve ordered source-target pairs for each function template. Keeping source and target within one category also keeps the surrounding computation applicable: a country exchanged for another country still has a capital, a language, and a continent.

concepts.name: Swapping more than one direction
concepts.summary: The construction extends past a single pair of vectors: several source coordinates can be exchanged for several target coordinates in one intervention.
concepts.explanation: The method is stated for $V = [v_s\;v_t]$, but several experiments permute more than two coordinates at once. In the Chinese antonym prompt the English lens coordinates for big and bigger are exchanged together for long and longer. In the bandit prompt the swap removes each condition's own strategy directions and installs the other condition's, so a small set of vectors moves as a block. In the character-counting experiment the swap maps every count in the forties to the corresponding value in the sixties, permuting a whole band of number tokens. In each case $V$ collects every direction involved and $\sigma$ is a permutation over their coordinates; the component of the activation orthogonal to the span of all of them is still left untouched.

concepts.name: The target-appropriate answer
concepts.summary: A swap is scored against the answer the prompt would have had if the swapped-in concept were the true one, not against the swapped-in concept itself.
concepts.explanation: The swap succeeds when the model outputs whatever the downstream computation should produce from the new argument. Exchanging spider for ant is scored on the output changing from 8 to 6, not on the model saying ant. In the arithmetic attribution graph, swapping the 42 node for 63 is scored on the probability of 70, because the +7 still follows it, while swapping the earlier 21 node for that same 63 is scored on 133, because the doubling and the addition both still follow. The threshold applied to this answer varies by experiment: top-1 of the output distribution in the internal-reasoning and flexible-generalization results, top-5 in the concept-vector variant of the report experiment, and a change in raw probability in the attribution-graph swaps, where the swap on the 7 operand raises the counterfactual answer substantially without displacing 49 as the top prediction.

concepts.name: Coordinates in a non-orthogonal frame
concepts.summary: J-lens vectors are neither orthogonal nor unit-norm, so the swap solves for the two coefficients with a pseudoinverse rather than taking plain inner products.
concepts.explanation: The rows of $W_U J_\ell$ form an overcomplete and correlated frame; the paper notes this when explaining why sparse decomposition returns a different set of active concepts than the top-$k$ inner products, and again when warning that the sparse decomposition behind the attribution graphs is not unique. Two lens vectors $v_s$ and $v_t$ will in general overlap, so $\langle v_s, h\rangle$ is not the amount of $v_s$ in $h$ once $v_t$ is also in play. The coordinates $c = V^\dagger h$ are instead the least-squares coefficients that best reproduce $h$ inside $\text{span}\{v_s, v_t\}$, and writing back $V(\sigma(c) - c)$ changes exactly those coefficients and nothing else. The informal description of the intervention as subtracting the projection onto the source vector and adding an equal-magnitude projection onto the target vector states the intent; the pseudoinverse is what makes it hold when the two directions are not perpendicular.

concepts.name: Reading a swap that does nothing
concepts.summary: A swap with no effect is used as evidence that a computation does not route through the J-space, though the paper also records that a failed swap can mean the concept was never strongly present.
concepts.explanation: Several results rest on an absence of effect. The Spanish-to-French swap leaves continuation and anomaly detection unmoved while flipping explicit report and flexible inference, and the swap mapping counts in the forties to counts in the sixties leaves the line-wrap point unchanged; both are read as those computations bypassing the J-space. In the arithmetic attribution graph, swapping the 17 or 4 coordinates has essentially no effect, which is read as the first addition happening outside the J-space. The limitations section records the competing reading: swap failures are concentrated where the source concept's lens vector was weakly active to begin with, one cause of which is that the model's working representation does not coincide with any single-token lens vector. The two readings are separated, where they are separated at all, by showing that the concept is present in the readout while the swap still does nothing, as in the language case where the language name appears in the lens at comparable rates in all four conditions.

concepts.name: Swapping the same value into different slots
concepts.summary: The same replacement value is written into two different intermediate nodes and produces two different answers, which the paper takes as showing each intermediate is operated on by the computation that follows it.
concepts.explanation: On the prompt "calc: ( 4 + 17 ) * 2 + 7 =", swapping the 42 node for 63 substantially raises the probability of 70, and swapping the earlier 21 node for that same 63 substantially raises the probability of 133. The difference is the doubling step, which lies downstream of 21 but not of 42. Because the value written in is identical in the two trials, the difference in output cannot come from the value; it comes from which slot received it. The paper uses this to argue that a named node holds a genuine intermediate that later computation consumes, rather than an early copy of the answer being pushed toward the output.

concepts.name: The per-trial swap grid
concepts.summary: Every swap trial of the flexible-generalization experiment is laid out as one 4x4 grid per function template, with rows the argument present in the prompt and columns the argument swapped in.
concepts.explanation: The diagonal of each grid is the unmodified baseline, since source and target coincide there, leaving 48 off-diagonal cells per category as actual swaps. Each cell shows the model's top-1 token after the swap, and where that is not the target-appropriate answer, a small grey number gives that answer's rank. The grids show how far the effect varies by category at $\alpha = 1$: country facts reach rank 1 in 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells, months succeed partially, animals rarely, and number relations in 0 of 48. Among the failures the top-1 output is usually still the answer for the original argument, with the target's answer further down the ranking, which the paper reads as the swap moving the activation in the right direction but not far enough.
